content: Systemic circulation refers to the part of the cardiovascular system responsible for transporting oxygen-rich blood from the heart to the rest of the body and returning oxygen-depleted blood back to the heart. This process is distinct from pulmonary circulation, which involves the exchange of gases in the lungs. In systemic circulation, arteries carry oxygenated blood to the tissues of the body. As blood flows through the capillaries, oxygen diffuses from the blood into the surrounding cells, while carbon dioxide diffuses from the cells into the blood. Veins then transport the deoxygenated blood back to the heart. Oxygenated blood enters the systemic circulation when it exits the left ventricle of the heart through the aortic semilunar valve. The blood is then pumped into the aorta, a large and thick-walled artery. The aorta arches and branches off into major arteries that supply the upper body. It then passes through the diaphragm to deliver blood to the lower parts of the body via its various branches. Blood flows from the arteries into capillaries, which are the smallest and most numerous blood vessels. These capillaries serve as the interface between the blood and the tissues, allowing the exchange of oxygen, nutrients, carbon dioxide, and waste products. While peripheral tissues extract oxygen from the blood, they do not completely deoxygenate it. As a result, venous blood still contains some oxygen, albeit at a lower concentration than arterial blood. At the same time, carbon dioxide and metabolic waste products are added to the blood. The deoxygenated blood is collected by small vessels called venules, which merge to form veins. The blood then flows into the two largest veins of the systemic circulation: the inferior vena cava, which drains blood from areas below the heart, and the superior vena cava, which drains blood from areas above the heart. These veins return the blood to the right atrium of the heart, completing the systemic circulation. The coronary sinus, which collects blood from the heart's own veins, also empties into the right atrium. From here, the blood enters the pulmonary circulation to be re-oxygenated before returning to the systemic circulation. This is a key advantage of systemic circulation compared to other forms of circulation, such as the open circulatory systems found in some invertebrates or the gill-based systems used by fish for respiration.
